paragraphs.heading: What makes a galaxy active
paragraphs.text: An active galaxy is one whose center hosts an active galactic nucleus, or AGN: a compact core that sends out a large amount of energy its stars cannot account for. This extra light shows up across the electromagnetic spectrum. It has been seen in radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.

paragraphs.heading: The engine at the center
paragraphs.text: Astronomers have proposed that the light comes from accretion, the gathering of matter by a supermassive black hole at the galaxy's center. Such black holes are put at 10⁶ to 10¹⁰ times the Sun's mass. Accretion can turn energy into radiation very efficiently, which can explain how a compact core stays so bright for so long. Supermassive black holes are now thought to sit in the centers of most if not all massive galaxies. So a galaxy is expected to show AGN-like features whenever a supply of material comes within reach of its central black hole.

paragraphs.heading: Why they look different
paragraphs.text: Active galaxies do not all look alike. What we see depends on the black hole's mass, how fast gas feeds it, the orientation of its disk, how much dust hides the core, and whether jets are present. Astronomers have defined many subclasses from these observed differences. The most powerful are classed as quasars, and a blazar is one whose jet points toward Earth, its light strengthened by relativistic beaming.

paragraphs.heading: Seyfert galaxies
paragraphs.text: Signs of activity turned up in photographs during the first half of the 20th century, before anyone understood the cause. Edward Fath published emission lines from the cores of NGC 1068 and Messier 81 in 1909, and Heber Curtis published the discovery of the jet in Messier 87 in 1918. In 1943 Carl Seyfert described nearby galaxies with bright cores giving off unusually broad emission lines, among them NGC 1068 and NGC 4151. Galaxies like these are now called Seyfert galaxies in his honor.

paragraphs.heading: Radio galaxies and quasars
paragraphs.text: Radio astronomy was a major push toward understanding active galaxies. Some of the earliest radio sources found were active elliptical galaxies close to us, including Messier 87 and Centaurus A. Other radio sources looked almost like single points of light and were named quasi-stellar radio sources, later shortened to quasars. In 1963 Maarten Schmidt measured the redshift of the quasar 3C 273 and noted that, if it lay far outside the Milky Way, it had to be the central region of a galaxy roughly 100 times as powerful as the radio galaxies identified before. Such enormous outputs meant ordinary stars could not be the power source.

paragraphs.heading: Our galaxy and the wider universe
paragraphs.text: The supermassive black hole at the center of the Milky Way is not active now, but it is thought to have been active about 8 billion years ago. In 1969 Donald Lynden-Bell proposed that the supermassive black holes in the centers of nearby galaxies are relics of dead quasars. Active nuclei are the most luminous lasting sources of radiation in the universe, so they help astronomers find distant objects. How they changed over cosmic time also limits which models of the cosmos can be right.
